item.title: Toward Self-Healing Engineering Systems
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Bari Syed
item.description: Applied carefully, agentic AI makes automation adaptive—not simply faster.
item.content:encoded:
In more than 20 years of QA automation and network security engineering across financial services, healthcare, pharmaceuticals, semiconductor design, and next-generation firewall testing, automation has meant teaching machines to follow instructions we already understand.

That model speeds delivery, but struggles with situations its designers did not anticipate.

Tests fail when APIs change, interface elements move, or environments behave unexpectedly. Some failures are intermittent, caused by asynchronous waits, concurrency, or test-order dependencies. The framework reports the failure; a human still diagnoses it.

Agentic AI introduces a different approach. An agent observes a system, reasons about what it sees, plans an action, checks the result, and continues until the task succeeds or human help is needed. Applied carefully, this makes automation adaptive—not simply faster.

From Automated Execution to Autonomous Reasoning

Traditional automation follows a fixed sequence: Trigger → Execute → Verify → Report. Agentic automation adds a reasoning loop: Observe → Reason → Plan → Act → Verify → Learn or Escalate. That change may look small, but it alters the engineering problem.

If a test cannot find a button, a conventional framework reports “Element not found.” An agent could compare page versions, identify a changed identifier, verify that the business function still works, then propose an updated locator and rerun the test.

This is self-healing test automation, but the term needs care. A system that edits its own tests and declares success is not necessarily intelligent or safe. The objective is not simply to make a test pass. It is to identify why it failed, make the smallest justified correction, and provide evidence that the correction is valid.

A Failing Test Is Not Necessarily a Defect

A red test does not automatically mean the application is broken. In network security testing, failure may originate in the device, traffic generator, lab topology, test, or an external dependency.

After an overnight deployment, a customer-order suite fails. The cause might be a changed API, obsolete locator, consumed test data, unavailable dependency, expired token, partial deployment, or genuine defect. A traditional framework may report them all alike.

An agent can correlate logs, traces, deployment records, code changes, test history, and environment health. It might report that the customer-status endpoint changed its response structure, moving an expected field, and that three other tests failed after the same deployment.

That is a meaningful shift—from detecting failure to diagnosing it.

The Self-Healing Loop

Self-healing should operate as a controlled feedback loop:

  • Observe: Gather test results, logs, traces, and environment signals.
  • Diagnose: Separate application defects from test or environment problems.
  • Plan: Choose the smallest, lowest-risk correction.
  • Act: Make only an authorized change.
  • Validate: Rerun the test and related checks.
  • Accept or escalate: Record evidence or send the issue to an engineer.

Every repair should pass a confidence and policy gate. A failed gate should lead to escalation, not another unreviewed attempt.

Evidence Before Action

There is a temptation to describe agentic AI as fully autonomous software engineering. I am more cautious. If loosening a payment validation rule makes a failing test pass, the green result may conceal a serious defect. Before accepting an automated repair, I would require evidence that:

  • The failure is reproducible and the change addresses its cause.
  • The repaired test passes repeatedly, as do related tests.
  • Business behavior, security, and compliance requirements remain intact.
  • The change is within the agent’s authorized scope.

The agent should not be rewarded simply for producing a green pipeline. It should be evaluated on whether the pipeline is trustworthy.

What Agents Should Automate First

Four areas offer value while preserving engineering control.

Test maintenance: Identify obsolete locators, changed API contracts, unstable tests, and broken test data; recommend or make low-risk updates.

Test generation: Draft tests from requirements, APIs, and past defects. Engineers must check that they cover meaningful behavior, not just mirror implementation.

Regression optimization: Use change information and test history to select relevant tests without sacrificing critical coverage.

Failure triage: Classify failures as new, known, environmental, intermittent, or likely regressions. This may deliver the greatest early value by separating infrastructure noise from product defects.

The shift is from asking, “Which test should I execute?” to asking, “What evidence do I need to decide whether this change is safe?”

Self-Healing Does Not Mean Human-Free

The future does not remove engineers from the process; it changes where they spend their time. No engineer should have to fix the same broken locator repeatedly. Engineers should, however, define what an agent is allowed to change.

I see three practical levels of autonomy:

  • Low risk: The agent can act automatically on reversible, well-understood changes.
  • Medium risk: The agent proposes a change and an engineer approves it.
  • High risk: Changes involving security, financial transactions, customer data, production infrastructure, or business-critical behavior require explicit human authorization.

Test engineers increasingly become designers of quality systems. Their expertise moves toward risk modeling, observability, reliability, security, and defining what evidence is sufficient to establish confidence.

From Self-Healing Tests to Self-Healing Systems

The same principles can extend beyond testing. One agent might connect rising latency to a recent deployment and recommend a rollback. Another might generate tests when an API contract change affects downstream consumers. A security agent might investigate unusual access patterns and recommend containment.

I think of these as intelligent engineering loops: systems that continuously observe software, reason about its behavior, take controlled actions, and verify the consequences. The goal is not software that blindly repairs itself. It is software that can correct problems within defined boundaries and produce evidence people can trust.

The Engineering Challenge Ahead

Writing another test script is no longer the hardest part. The challenge is the control system: observability, authorization boundaries, auditability, secure tool access, rollback, repeatable validation, and confidence measures.

Organizations must avoid excessive agency: granting more permissions or autonomy than a task requires. Fewer human interventions are not automatically better; success means reducing unnecessary intervention while preserving quality, safety, security, and accountability.

A New Role for Software Engineers

Software engineering has moved from manual testing to scripted automation, from scripted deployments to continuous delivery, and from hand-managed servers to infrastructure as code. The next transition may be from deterministic automation to adaptive engineering systems.

That makes experience more important, not obsolete. An agent can generate thousands of actions, but it still needs engineering judgment to decide which actions are safe. Engineers who understand failure modes, distributed systems, security, and business risk are well positioned to build and govern these systems.

The future I see is not AI replacing engineers. It is engineers building systems in which agents help us test, repair, and improve software. The real measure of success will not be how autonomous these systems become, but how much more reliable software engineering becomes because we learned to make autonomy trustworthy.

Disclosure: Generative AI tools, including Anthropic’s Claude, were used to help condense an earlier draft, identify and check supporting references, and edit for clarity. The ideas, examples, technical arguments, and conclusions are the author’s own, drawn from his professional experience. The author reviewed the final text and takes full responsibility for its content and references.


Mohammed Bari Syed is a Principal Network QA Engineer at Palo Alto Networks, with more than 20 years of experience in QA automation and network security engineering. The views expressed here are his own and do not represent those of his employer.

item.title: Beyond Model Alignment: The Case for Bounded Autonomy in AI Systems
item.dc:creator: Daniel Khashabi
item.description: The goal of “perfectly aligned” models is elusive if not impossible.
item.content:encoded:
We are caught in a dilemma: Full autonomy risks ungovernable behavior, while pure control collapses AI into mere software, forfeiting the value of autonomous action.9 The answer to that dilemma has largely been framed as a model alignment problem. If we can instill the right values into a model—through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF),3 constitutional training,2 or similar techniques—the thinking goes, we would end up with a “good” model that will behave well across all contexts. As Anthropic CEO and co-founder Dario Amodei puts it, “We believe that a feasible goal for 2026 is to train Claude in such a way that it almost never goes against the spirit of its constitution.”1

We argue that this approach is risky. For a broad range of reasons we detail below, the goal of “perfectly aligned” models is elusive if not impossible. Even Amodei hedges his statement by talking about the “spirit” of alignment and acknowledging that misalignment will occur “almost never.” In the same essay, he enumerates instances of Claude engaging in deception, blackmail, and reward-hacking during internal testing. The architect of Constitutional AI is, in effect, conceding a central point: Alignment cannot be relied upon as a guarantee of safe behavior. With AI autonomy, even a single misaligned action can cause tremendous damage.

Summer Yue, director of alignment at Meta Superintelligence Labs, provided a compelling example. She had instructed her agent to confirm before acting; instead, it began deleting every message in her inbox more than a week old. “I couldn’t stop it from my phone. I had to [run] to my Mac mini like I was defusing a bomb.”a If even an alignment researcher cannot control their own agent, the risks are far greater for ordinary users.

We propose a complementary principle: bounded autonomy (BA), a proposal motivated by the hypothesis that model alignment will never be perfect and failure is expected. Therefore, BA shifts part of the safety burden from “aligned models” to “safe systems” that constrain agent authority. Even when both pursue the same ultimate safety goal, they place the safety guarantee in different parts of the system.

Autonomy without Boundaries in the Wild

To see what happens when autonomy operates within minimal authority boundaries, consider what happened when a human user deployed “MJ Rathbun,” an AI agent tasked to act as an autonomous scientific coder: find bugs in open source projects, fix them, and open pull requests. The human operator’s involvement was minimal by design. Their instructions were deliberately hands-off: When the agent asked for guidance, the operator’s typical reply was “you respond, don’t ask me”7—effectively granting the agent unbounded autonomy.

MJ Rathbun eventually submitted a code change to a widely used library. When the library’s maintainers rejected the pull request, the agent researched the maintainer’s personal information online, presented hallucinated details as fact, and then published a blog post accusing them of discrimination and prejudice.

A more recent example is the OpenAI agents’ attack on HuggingFace infrastructure. During a multi-day evaluation of cyber capabilities, models ran with reduced safeguards inside what OpenAI researchers believed was a bounded sandbox. The agents used a shared package-registry cache as an unauthorized message board, pooled fragments of information across separate evaluation runs, obtained Internet access, and reached into HuggingFace’s production network.5

There are two important lessons in these stories: First, while these anecdotes may sound like edge cases, they are a preview of how humans and organizations will increasingly use AI agents with more autonomy, less oversight. Second, in both cases, the underlying models were frontier language models that had already gone through extensive alignment training, and yet none of that alignment prevented the outcome.

Unattainability of Perfect Model Alignment (and the Necessity of BA)

The dominant paradigm for AI safety today is alignment: the effort to instill values directly into model weights so that good behavior becomes an intrinsic property of the system. Virtually every major AI company—Anthropic, OpenAI, Google—relies on some variant of alignment training to instill safety principles into model weights. The underlying premise is appealing: If we can train a model to be “good” by reliably acting in accordance with human values, safety follows from the model itself.

We believe this premise, taken as the sole basis for safety, is unattainable—for several reasons:

The long tail of failures. Language models struggle with “long-tail” phenomenon failures: Rare but consequential failure modes are combinatorially large, and no amount of alignment training is likely to eliminate them entirely.4 The MJ Rathbun incident is a case in point: No training dataset anticipated the specific chain of events that led this AI agent to publish a defamatory blog post against a human.

We also know that problem complexity (and hence, the “long-tail”) compounds over a long horizon chain of decisions, which is typical of AI agents deployed in open-ended tasks such as executing convoluted research or coding tasks. Multiple agents compound the problem: The space of possible interactions grows multiplicatively, so the tail gets longer. This enlarges the alignment burden without changing what a well-placed bound must enforce.

Incomplete instructions. It is the nature of human-human communication to leave out details: We speak in shorthand and expect others to fill in the gaps sensibly based on shared context (culture, law, and social norms). Models, however, may not fill those gaps in the way a human operator expects.

Instructions can be incomplete due to social or pragmatic pressures. We delegate problems because we do not have time to specify every detail (as in the Rathbun operator’s instruction, “you respond, don’t ask me”), or because we do not know how to solve them ourselves (the case of cyberattacks). In such cases, misalignment means failing to make the right judgment when instructions are open-ended.

The world shifts, but models do not. A model that is aligned in one context may be misaligned in other operating conditions. One factor is time: Models trained on data and values of 2026 may be misaligned by 2027. Besides the temporal factor, the deployment context—policies of each organization, norms of each culture, laws of different jurisdictions—shifts the guardrails that ought to be imposed. A one-size-fits-all aligned model cannot satisfy all of them simultaneously.

Training models to be helpful, harmless, and honest is clearly desirable. But relying on alignment as the primary guarantee of safety is analogous to relying solely on pilots for aviation safety while doing away with air traffic control, flight checklists, and the rest of the aviation safety ecosystem.

From Models to Systems

The alignment paradigm focuses on the model—the neural network that maps inputs to outputs. But AI is increasingly deployed as systems that wrap models within orchestration layers that govern their interaction with the world.

While the focus of AI development has moved decisively from models to systems, the AI safety mainstream remains focused on model alignment, and system-level safety practices remain ad hoc. MJ Rathbun’s harmful behavior or the OpenAI/HuggingFace incident did not stem from a lack of alignment, as in both cases the underlying model was almost certainly a frontier model that had already undergone alignment training. The failure was insufficient system-level constraints on the agent’s actions.

Bounded Autonomy

The core claim of BA is simple: Just as modern software engineering assumes bugs will exist and builds testing and monitoring infrastructure accordingly, BA assumes that model misbehavior should be treated as an expected condition. Therefore, BA focuses on shaping structured freedom into what the system is allowed to do: creating a space where agents can act freely yet remain within explicitly defined safety boundaries.

The boundaries are not learned or internalized in the model, but rather they are engineered, auditable, and revisable by the system designer. This is different from—and complementary to—the current dominant paradigm that internalizes values (à la Constitution) into the model itself.2 This is also different from blindly severing an agent’s connections to the world (aka “sandboxing”). Sandboxing is one mechanism within a broader set of levers that can be used to shape the engagement with the outside world and the autonomy envelope.

Establishing BA as a principle is a first step, but research is needed to elaborate and refine that principle. Many such principles are possible; we highlight three here:

  • Bounds must be operational: A boundary that says “the system should be fair” is aspirational. A boundary that says “the system may not make hiring decisions without human review” is closer to being operational. BA demands the latter: enforceable constraints that can be verified and audited.

  • Bounds must be configurable: While alignment typically aims for a universal standard of “good” behavior, BA treats governance as inherently contextual: different users, organizations, and regulatory environments should be able to define, adjust, and contextualize boundaries depending on purpose, risk, or domain. A medical AI assistant in a teaching hospital may operate under different autonomy bounds than the same system deployed in a rural clinic.

  • Bounds must be set from outside the agent’s control: A bound the agent can widen is not a bound. Authority is granted by the system and cannot be acquired by the agent, however it reasons. A self-driving car picks the lane and the speed, but the passenger picks the destination. The car does not get to decide mid-route that a different trip would be more useful, and it cannot grant itself permission to drive on the sidewalk. An AI agent should act freely inside its envelope and have no mechanism for enlarging it. Where wider authority is legitimately needed, it is issued by a human or by a separate authorizing system that the agent does not control.

A related prior work we highlight is the “adjustable autonomy” of Scerri, Pynadath, and Tambe,6 which addresses when an agent should transfer decision-making control to a human by optimizing over transfer-of-control strategies via MDPs under the assumption of a faithful agent. BA, by contrast, assumes model misbehavior is an expected condition and imposes externally enforced constraints on what the agent is permitted to do.

How BA should be operationalized is itself an open research question—and arguably the central one. What follows is not a blueprint but a first attempt to characterize the design space. We offer it to motivate the research agenda, not to foreclose it.

Designing bounded autonomy: A layered defense.

We distinguish three categories of safety intervention. Category 1 consists of guardrails built into the model itself via the dominant training-based paradigms. Category 2 consists of external classifiers and monitors deployed on top of the model, which monitor inputs and outputs for unsafe content. Category 3 consists of hard, unconditional constraints that are non-negotiable regardless of context or reasoning—authorization rules such as “never use the user’s credit card without explicit confirmation” or “never delete a file without first creating a backup.” This also includes sandboxes, VMs, file-system boundaries, and network egress controls.

Bounded autonomy argues for moving beyond overreliance on Category 1, and for expanding serious engineering effort around Categories 2 and 3.

One way to think about how these categories fit together is as layers in a Swiss cheese model. Category 1 sits at the first layer. Surrounding it are multiple layers of Category 2 classifiers, each tuned to different safety considerations and sensitivity levels. Category 3 forms the outermost boundary, holding regardless of what any inner layer permits. No single layer is perfect, but the combination is substantially more robust. The goal is to engineer a system in which the layers collectively leave nearly no gaps.

The empirical results support layering safety modules. Adding Category 2 guardrails on top of an already-aligned model (Category 1) improves safety with a negligible increase in over-refusals and compute overhead.8 A further practical advantage is modularity: Safety layers can be updated without retraining the model, allowing targeted responses when a specific adversarial attack bypasses model-level alignment. In the OpenAI cybersecurity incident, OpenAI’s own reporting confirmed that the propensity to compromise infrastructure drops more than a hundredfold when the same models run with the production scaffold that enforces the oversight of cybersecurity classifiers.5

The multi-layered architecture implicitly characterizes the system’s safe operating boundaries. A useful analogy is the aviation flight envelope. Aircraft are not designed to fly in all conditions. Instead, they define the limits within which the system operates reliably. BA asks the same of AI systems: auditable boundaries that place the safety-utility trade-off in the hands of the designers rather than leaving it implicit in the model’s weights.

Crucially, just having layers is not enough: The safe operating envelope of an agentic system must be calibrated to the actual capabilities of the underlying model(s). Bounds set too loosely fail to prevent harm; bounds set too tightly waste the potential of capable models and may themselves degrade outcomes. A core part of the BA research agenda is therefore developing rigorous methods for characterizing the right envelope for a given agent, task class, and deployment context.

One might ask: If leading labs already layer classifiers on top of aligned models, what does BA add? Current practice remains ad hoc and fragmented across alignment, AI control, access privileges, and containment. This is a call for developing principled frameworks for characterizing the autonomy envelope of AI agents.

A taxonomy of constraints.

With these design choices in mind, we sketch a taxonomy of constraint types, proceeding from the most granular level outward to broader restrictions. Each constraint embodies a trade-off: It increases safety while limiting utility. Further research is required to ensure systems do not circumvent these constraints in practice. This taxonomy should therefore be understood not as a specification of BA, but as the basis for a research program.

Action constraints.  Reversibility constraints apply cautious engineering to AI behavior: only allow autonomous actions that can be undone. An agent may draft an email but not send it or flag a file for deletion but not delete it permanently. Reversibility should be a first-class attribute in any BA specification and maps naturally onto existing software patterns—transactions, staging environments, and version control. Irreversible actions should be prohibited or escalated for human review.

Whitelists and blacklists are complementary mechanisms for managing permitted actions. A whitelist defines authorized actions and prohibits everything else by default, consistent with least privilege; a blacklist prohibits specific actions and permits everything else. For high-risk agents, whitelisting is strongly preferable. The two can be layered: a whitelist of permitted tool classes combined with blacklists of specific prohibited operations within each class.

Metric constraints.  Time-to-live (TTL) constraints bound the temporal duration of an agent’s authorization. As Zittrain proposed, authority granted to an agent should not persist indefinitely.10 An agent dispatched for a two-hour task should not retain broad access for two weeks. TTL constraints address the accumulation of latent agency in systems granted permissions once and never revoked; when authorization decays automatically, the damage radius of a dormant or compromised agent contracts over time.

Expenditure constraints establish hard limits on the financial resources an agent can deploy—among the most straightforward constraints to implement and the most practically important. An agent capped at one hundred dollars cannot directly spend a million. More broadly, resource-consumption constraints cap expenses of various forms: API calls, compute, storage, bandwidth and so forth.

Scope constraints bound the geographic or jurisdictional scope of an agent. The digital world already encodes such constraints implicitly (e.g., data residency laws, export controls). An agent handling European health data, for example, should be prohibited from transmitting data outside GDPR-compliant jurisdictions. Spatial constraints are particularly important for multi-agent systems, where information can propagate across jurisdictional or infrastructure boundaries in ways the original agent did not anticipate.

Information-flow constraints.

Information-flow constraints govern how information may propagate. They track confidentiality, integrity, and provenance of what moves between an agent, its tools, and the outside world. The danger is a sequence of individually permissible actions that jointly produces a forbidden outcome. An agent blocked from a prohibited action may achieve the same outcome through individually permitted steps—gradually leaking sensitive information through multiple innocuous disclosures. Enforcement must therefore reason not only about atomic actions but also about trajectories of actions across sessions. This remains an open research problem, and one that grows more important as agents’ capabilities grow.

Domain constraints.  Functional domain constraints restrict an agent to a defined subject matter or organizational function. A financial analysis agent, for example, should have no access to employee communications or source code. This implements the principle of least privilege at the system level and enables configurability: The same model, instantiated with different domain constraints, can serve finance, legal review, or customer support, with boundaries enforced architecturally rather than relying on the model to “know its place.”

Composing the constraint taxonomy.

These categories act as layers. A well-designed BA system applies multiple constraints simultaneously, each protecting against a different failure class. An agent managing financial operations might face a whitelist of permitted API calls, an expenditure cap, a TTL on authorization, and a prohibition on accessing systems outside the finance domain. Any behavior exceeding this combined envelope is blocked or escalated at the system level, regardless of what the model decides.

This composability is itself a design principle. BA architectures should be built from modular, independently enforceable constraint components that can be combined, audited, and revised without the need to significantly modify the underlying model. While the model’s capabilities may evolve in ways that are hard to fully characterize, the constraint envelope should remain under explicit human control.

Enforcement belongs at the resource. A household circuit breaker trips at the panel when total draw exceeds its rating; it does not care how many appliances are plugged in, how they are wired, or whether they coordinate. Agent bounds should work the same way. A $500 account limit cannot be bypassed by one agent making ten $100 charges or ten agents making one charge each. If either evades the cap, the cap was implemented in the wrong place, for example, per session rather than at the account. That is an implementation error, not a reason to invent a new class of constraint.

A harder case is when agents work their way to acquire new authority. An agent capped at $500 may instead open a second account. An agent with no communication channel may assemble one out of storage it is allowed to write to, as OpenAI’s agents did with a shared package-registry cache. Neither move violates any single constraint, yet both leave the agent with authority nobody granted it. BA therefore requires that the power to grant authority sits outside the agent and that the system monitors for acquired privileges that expand the intended autonomy envelope.

Epilogue—and a Call to Arms

As AI agents become more capable and more deeply embedded in consequential decisions, the future of safe AI will not be defined by “perfectly aligned” models. It will be defined by systems whose autonomy is deliberately, transparently, and configurably bounded.

We call on the AI research community, industry practitioners, and policymakers to establish BA as a foundational principle for the era of AI agents. The AI safety research community should expand its focus beyond model-level alignment to developing system-level guarantees for specifying and verifying autonomy boundaries. For policymakers, it means shifting regulatory focus to AI systems operating within auditable autonomy envelopes.

Since this article was first drafted (late 2025), this system-level BA perspective has become increasingly visible. The frontier labs now regularly describe sandboxing, access controls, monitoring, and approval policies as core parts of agent safety. These are positive steps toward BA, but we are at the beginning of the road: We need principled frameworks for agent authority specification, composition, calibration, enforcement and verification.

item.title: The Randomized k-Server Conjecture Is False!
item.dc:creator: Sébastien Bubeck
item.description: In this paper, we refute the randomized k-server conjecture, which states that the randomized competitive ratio for the problem in all metric spaces (with at least k+1 points) is Θ(logk).
item.content:encoded:
Abstract

We prove a few new lower bounds on the randomized competitive ratio for the k-server problem and other related problems, resolving some long-standing conjectures. In particular, for metrical task systems (MTS), we asymptotically settle the competitive ratio and obtain the first improvement to an existential lower bound since the introduction of the model in 1987. More concretely, we show:
    1. There exist (k + 1)-point metric spaces in which the randomized competitive ratio for the k-server problem is Ω(log2k). This refutes the folklore conjecture (which is known to hold in some families of metrics) that in all metric spaces with at least k + 1 points, the competitive ratio is Θ(logk).
    2. Consequently, there exist n-point metric spaces in which the randomized competitive ratio for MTS is Ω(log2n). This matches the upper bound that holds for all metrics. The previously best existential lower bound was Ω(logn), which was known to be tight for some families of metrics.
    3. For all k < n ∈ ℕ, for all n-point metric spaces the randomized k-server competitive ratio is at least Ω(logk), and consequently the randomized MTS competitive ratio is at least Ω(logn). These universal lower bounds are asymptotically tight. The previous bounds were Ω(logk/log log k) and Ω(log n/log log n), respectively.
    4. Our results imply improved lower bounds for other problems, such as layered graph traversal, k-taxi, distributed paging, and metric allocation.
    These lower bounds share a common thread, and other than the third bound, also a common construction.

1. Introduction

Since its inception in the work of Manasse et al.,22 the k-server problem has been the driving challenge in shaping research on competitive analysis of online algorithms, a computing paradigm pioneered by Sleator and Tarjan.26 The problem is simple to state. (See Section 2 for descriptions of all the problems discussed in the introduction.) There are compellingly beautiful conjectures regarding the competitive ratio for deterministic and randomized algorithms. The attempts, partly successful, to prove these conjectures have led to the development of powerful tools whose impact reaches far beyond the k-server problem, or online computing for that matter. These include the application of and the contribution to concepts such as the work function, quasi-convexity, online choice of online algorithms, hierarchically separated trees (HSTs), non-contracting Lipschitz maps of metric spaces, metric Ramsey theory, the online primal-dual schema, entropic regularization, and the online mirror descent schema.

In this paper, we refute the randomized k-server conjecture, which states that the randomized competitive ratio for the problem in all metric spaces (with at least k+1 points) is Θ(logk). We construct, for all k∈N, metric spaces on k+1 points in which the randomized competitive ratio for this problem is Ω(log2k). This also implies stronger lower bounds for a number of related problems. In particular, the k-server problem in a (k+1)-point metric space is a special case of the metrical task systems problem in the same metric space.7 Therefore, we get that there are, for all n∈N, n-point metric spaces in which the randomized competitive ratio for the metrical task systems problem is Ω(log2n). Other problems whose lower bounds are improved as a result of our work include layered graph traversal,25 the k-taxi problem,16,13 distributed paging (a.k.a. constrained file allocation),4 and metric allocation.2 Details on these reductions can be found in the full version of our paper.

The results for the k-server and related problems are quite surprising. The new k-server lower bounds are asymptotically tight for k+1 point metric spaces, and more generally this is true of our metrical task systems lower bounds. Matching upper bounds were proved by Bubeck et al.10 and Coester and Lee.15 Previously, it has been widely conjectured that in all metric spaces on more than k points, the randomized competitive ratio for the k-server problem is Θ(logk), and this was established in some special cases. The best-known upper bounds for general metrics are O(log2klogn) and O(log3klogΔ),11 where n is the number of points in the metric space and Δ is the ratio between the largest and smallest non-zero distance, and O(k) by using a deterministic algorithm20 when both n and Δ are very large. Moreover, the deterministic k-server conjecture, which states that in every metric space on at least k+1 points the deterministic competitive ratio is exactly k, is nearly resolved. A lower bound of k is known to hold in all metrics.22 It is tight in many special cases,12,14,17 and it is within a factor of 2–1k of the truth in all cases.20 Thus, it was unexpected that in the randomized case the competitive ratio would vary widely among different metric spaces. Similarly, for metrical task systems, in some metric spaces an asymptotically tight Θ(logn) bound is known. It has been conjectured that this is the truth in all metric spaces (similar to the deterministic case, where all metric spaces are known to be equally hard with a competitive ratio of exactly 2n–17). Obviously, our results refute this conjecture.

Existential and universal lower bounds.

The previous best existential lower bound for metrical task systems, Ω(logn), was already proved in 1987 when the model was introduced.7 It uses a coupon collector argument, and the analogous proof had also remained the previously best existential lower bound for the k-server problem. In contrast, the best-known universal lower bounds (i.e., lower bounds that hold for all metrics) had developed over time: Initially it seemed plausible that there might even exist metric spaces with constant competitive ratio, until a first super-constant universal lower bound was shown in Karloff et al.19 This was based on the idea of showing that every metric space contains a large subspace belonging to a family for which a super-constant lower bound is known. This idea was developed further by Blum et al.6 and Bartal et al.,3,5 eventually resulting in lower bounds of Ω(logn/loglogn) and Ω(logk/loglogk), respectively, for metrical task systems and the k-server problem for all metric spaces of n>k points. These lower bounds are implied by an Ω(logn) lower bound on metrical task systems in Ω(log2n)-HST metrics from Bartal et al.3 in combination with lower bounds on the size of a subspace close to such a structure in any metric space from Bartal et al.5 We close the remaining gap to the upper bounds of O(logn) and O(logk) that hold in some metrics by proving universal lower bounds of Ω(logn) and Ω(logk), respectively. We show that such lower bounds hold for all 1-HST metrics. The universal lower bounds are then implied from Bartal et al.5 For details on this construction, we refer to the full version of our paper.

Overview of the existential lower bound proof.

Our existential lower bounds use a construction of a metric space akin to the diamond graph used by Newman and Rabinovich,24 Brinkman and Charikar,8 Lee and Naor,21 Mendel and Naor,23 and Andoni et al.1 to prove lower bounds on bi-Lipschitz distortion of metric embeddings and dimension reduction in ℓ1, and by Imase and Waxman18 to prove lower bounds on the online Steiner tree problem. The main idea is demonstrated by the following basic construction used in Section 3 to illustrate a somewhat weaker, yet simpler lower bound than our main result. We use the shortest path metric on the nodes of an inductively constructed graph. Let w∈N. The w graph is constructed as follows. Take a cycle whose length is a multiple of six. Let s and t be two antipodal points in this cycle. They partition the cycle into two s–t paths whose length is a multiple of three. We will consider the first, second, and last third of both paths. But first, we replace every edge in this graph with a copy of the w–1 graph, identifying the endpoints of the edge with the two chosen terminals of the recursive graph. Note that in an n-point metric space, if k=n–1, then the movement of the servers can be defined alternatively as the movement of the “hole,” a.k.a. anti-server—the unique position that no server occupies. The anti-server can be forced to choose a location from a subset of the points by requesting repeatedly the other points.

Now, we describe the bad sequence of requests, informally. Our argument uses Yao’s minimax principle—we design a random request sequence that drives the cost of every deterministic algorithm to reach or exceed the lower bound, which we denote here as Cw. This is done in three stages. The first stage  ensures the anti-server traverses the first third of one of the two s–t paths (which now consist of chains of w–1 graphs), while paying a factor of Cw–1 over the shortest path to this goal. The main purpose of this stage is to create two targets to choose from which are far apart. The last third is a mirror image of the first third and is intended to ensure the anti-server reaches t, while paying the same factor Cw–1 over the shortest path to that goal. The middle third is where the increase in the competitive ratio happens. There we repeatedly, independently, and with equal probability choose one of the two paths and force the anti-server either to move forward on the chosen path or to stay put on the other path. This is repeated for the length of the middle third, so in expectation, wherever the anti-server lies, it has to advance half the length of this interval. The initial distance gained from s guarantees that switching paths does not save any cost. Moreover, in expectation one of the two options “suffered” fewer “hits,” roughly square root of the number of repetitions fewer. We now take advantage of this expected gap and generate more requests that force the anti-server to use “the road less traveled by” and move there all the way to t. The excess steps force Cw to be at least Cw–1+Θ(Cw–1), and this shows an Ω(w2) lower bound. Finally, the size of this graph is exp(wlogw), so this argument gives Ω((logk/loglogk)2). To improve the latter bound, we need to “compress” the graph to use cycles of length six, recursively, so its size is exp(w). This complicates the argument considerably. As the graph is symmetric with respect to the roles of s and t, we can then reverse the process (now going from t to s) and thus repeat it as many times as desired.

2. Preliminaries

An online (minimization) problem is a two-player game between an adversary and an online algorithm. Keeping the discussion somewhat informal, the adversary chooses a finite sequence of requests ρ=ρ[1]ρ[2]ρ[3]…. The algorithm chooses a response function alg that maps every request sequence to an action. When the game is played, the algorithm responds to each request ρ[i] with alg[i]=alg(ρ[1]ρ[2]…ρ[i]), thus generating a response sequence alg=alg[1]alg[2]alg[3]… (abusing notation slightly). A randomized algorithm alg~ chooses alg from a probability distribution on such functions. Thus, a play of the game is marked by a pair of equal-length sequences (ρ,alg). For each pair of an algorithm and request sequence there is an associated cost. We denote by calg(ρ) the cost of algorithm alg on request sequence ρ, and by copt(ρ)=minalg{calg(ρ)} the cost of the optimal (offline) algorithm.

Definition 1.

The randomized competitive ratio of an online problem ONL, denoted CrandONL, is the infimum over all C that satisfy the following condition. There exists a randomized algorithm alg~ and some constant κ such that for every adversary strategy ρ, E[calg(ρ):alg∼alg~]≤C·copt(ρ)+κ.

Unless stated otherwise, the constant κ can be arbitrary. However, for some problems it is more typical to require κ=0.

Definition 2.

The distributional lower bound on the randomized competitive ratio of an online problem ONL, denoted CdistrONL, is the supremum over all C that satisfy the following condition. For all κ (which are allowed in Definition 1), there is a probability distribution ρ~ over adversary strategies such that for every (deterministic) algorithm alg, E[calg(ρ):ρ∼ρ~]≥C·E[copt(ρ):ρ∼ρ~]+κ.

The following theorem is known as Yao’s minimax principle.

Theorem 3 (Yao’s minimax).

CrandONL=CdistrONL.

Some notation.

Let ρ be a request sequence. We will use subscripts ρi to indicate subsequences in an underlying partition ρ=ρ1ρ2…ρm. Note that each ρi is a sequence, not necessarily a single request. We denote by ρ≤i the prefix ρ1ρ2…ρi. For two indices i≤j, we denote by ρi≤·≤j the subsequence ρiρi+1…ρj.

Escape prices.

Given an online problem ONL, we will sometimes consider an escape price relaxation of ONL, defined as follows. There is an underlying escape price parameter p≥0. At certain points in the request sequence (potentially all of them), the online algorithm is allowed as an additional option to respond to a request by bailing out of the game. If the online algorithm responds to a request ρ[t] by bailing out of the game, then the escape price p is added to its cost, but the online algorithm pays no additional cost for any requests thereafter (including the request ρ[t] itself). If we allow this additional option of bailing out only in response to requests ρ[t] belonging to some specific subsequence ρi≤·≤j, then we say that the escape price is available on ρi≤·≤j.

In the escape price relaxation of a problem, we allow invoking the escape price only to the online algorithm, but not to the (offline) algorithms defining the base cost. Thus, the escape price option only helps the online player, and the competitive ratio for the escape price relaxation of ONL is at most CrandONL, regardless of the value of p.

More notation.

In some online problems, there is an adjustable starting configuration s which affects the cost. Given a play (ρ,alg) with starting configuration s, we often write calg,s(ρ) to denote the cost of the algorithm in this case, and copt,s(ρ) for the corresponding optimal (offline) cost. Moreover, let ρ=ρ1ρ2 be the concatenation of two request sequences ρ1 and ρ2. For a play (ρ,alg) with starting configuration s, we write

c alg , s ( ρ 2 | ρ 1 ) : = c alg , s ( ρ ) – c alg , s ( ρ 1 ) ,

denoting the partial cost of the online algorithm on the subsequence ρ2 when serving the request sequence ρ=ρ1ρ2. When the initial location s is clear from the context, we will often drop it from the notation.

Now let us discuss the main online problems considered in this paper.

k-server.

There is an underlying metric space M=(M,d) with |M|>k. The adversary’s strategy ρ is a sequence of points ρ[1],ρ[2],…∈M. The algorithm controls k identical servers, initially located at k distinct points in M. The response alg[i] to a request ρ[i] moves one of the servers from its current location to ρ[i]. This adds to the cost of the algorithm the distance travelled by the server. We denote this problem as kSRV.

Metrical task systems.

Here, too, there is an underlying metric space M=(M,d). The elements of M are called states. An adversary’s request is a vector in (R+∪{∞})M, where R+ denotes the set of non-negative real numbers. The algorithm begins at an arbitrary alg[0]∈M. In response to ρ[i]∈(R+∪{∞})M, the algorithm must choose a state alg[i]∈M. This adds to its cost d(alg[i–1],alg[i])+ρ[i](alg[i]). We denote this problem as MTS.

Small set chasing.

There is an underlying metric space M=(M,d), and a starting point x0∈M. The adversary presents requests which are subsets of M, each of cardinality at most w. To serve a request, the algorithm must move to one of the points in the finite subset, incurring a cost equal to the distance traversed. We denote this problem by MSS. (The abbreviation stands for metrical service systems, which is the historical name of the problem.) The following relationships are known.

Proposition 4 (folklore).

Let M be an n-point metric space and let k=n–1. Then, for every w∈{1,2,…,k}, CrandMTS(M)≥CrandkSRV(M)≥CrandMSS(M,w). The second inequality is an equality if w=k.

Proof (Idea).

In (n–1)-server there is exactly one point not covered by a server, and this point corresponds to the server location in MSS and MTS. Then, a request to a set S⊂M in MSS corresponds to repeated k-server requests to all the points in MS. A k-server request at a point p∈M corresponds to the MTS cost vector that assigns cost ∞ to p and cost 0 to other points.

3. Basic Construction and Analysis

The main goal of this section is to describe, in a somewhat informal style, a simple construction and analysis which yields a lower bound of Ω((lognloglogn)2) for MSS in n-point metric spaces with request sets of arbitrary size. Notice that this lower bound implies immediately the same lower bound for MTS and for kSRV, putting k=n–1, on account of Proposition 4. In the full version of our paper, we show that this lower bound can also be achieved with request sets of size at most w=O(lognloglogn), which implies a lower bound of Ω(w2) for width-w layered graph traversal, matching the upper bound from Bubeck et al.9

3.1. The family of metric spaces.

First we describe our family of metric spaces by induction. Let m0≤m1≤m2≤⋯ be a sequence of natural numbers, to be determined later. We construct a sequence of finite metric spaces M0=(M0,d0), M1=(M1,d1), M2=(M2,d2), … of growing size as follows. Each metric in this sequence is the shortest-path metric of an underlying graph. The base case M0 is a single edge of weight 1. Next, M1 is a cycle with 6m0 edges. In other words, we form a cycle of 6m0 copies of M0. We also choose two special antipodal vertices/points s and t, so diam(M1)=d1(s,t).

More generally, Mw+1 is built from Mw in the same way as M1 was built from M0 (see Figure 1). Namely, Mw+1 is a “cycle” made of 6mw copies of Mw. Slightly more precisely, consider a cycle with 6mw edges, where each edge {u,v} is replaced by putting a copy of Mw with the two special vertices at u and v. In particular, in Mw+1, each special vertex of one copy of Mw is identified with another special vertex in another copy of Mw. In Mw+1, the special vertices s and t are special vertices in two distinct copies of Mw such that diam(Mw+1)=dw+1(s,t). Notice that Mw+1 can be viewed as consisting of a left path of 3mw copies of Mw and a right path of another 3mw copies of Mw. For two subsets of points S,S‘⊂Mw, we denote by (S,S‘,i,j) the subset of Mw+1 that is made of the union of the set S in the ith copy of Mw on the left path, and the set S‘ in the jth copy of Mw on the right path.

3.2. The hard sequence.

Now let us describe by induction a hard random sequence ρw of subsets of Mw. Recall that ρw[j] denotes the jth request in the sequence ρw. This is a random subset of Mw. Also let Tw denote the length of ρw. The construction gives Tw as a random variable, but for simplicity we ignore this aspect as we can always pad a sequence with some dummy sets to attain a fixed length. We will always have ρw[1] be the special vertex s (the source) and ρw[Tw] be the special vertex t (the target). Moreover, our construction will guarantee that the request sequence can be satisfied by following a shortest path connecting s and t (so copt(ρw) is simply the length of this path). We denote by ρw,1,ρw,2,⋯ a sequence of i.i.d. copies of ρw. The inductive construction of ρw+1 uses ρw and proceeds in three stages.

Stage 1.

For every i=1,⋯,mw and j∈{1,2,…,Tw}, let

ρ w + 1 [ ( i – 1 ) T w + j ] = ( ρ w , i [ j ] , ρ w , i [ j ] , i , i ) .

In words, we traverse simultaneously the first third of the left and right path of Mw+1, one copy of Mw at a time, using the hard sequence for Mw.

Stage 2.

For every i=1,⋯,mw, let ϵi∈{0,1} be a Bernoulli random variable independent of everything else. Let left(i)=mw+ϵ1+⋯+ϵi, and let right(i)=mw+(1–ϵ1)+⋯+(1–ϵi). Now, for every j∈{1,2,…,Tw}, let

In words, if ϵi=1, we present the hard sequence on the next copy of Mw on the left path, and on the right path we “stay put” (i.e., we keep requesting the target of the last copy of Mw that was previously traversed). Conversely, if ϵi=0 we “stay put” on the left path, and on the right path we traverse the next copy of Mw using the hard sequence. (Recall that always ρw[Tw]={t}.)

Stage 3.

Assume that left(mw)≥right(mw)—the other case is dealt with by symmetry. Then, for i=1,⋯,3mw–right(mw) and j=1,2,…,Tw, we set

ρ w + 1 [ ( 2 m w + i – 1 ) T w + j ] = ( ∅ , ρ w , 2 m w + i [ j ] , 1 , right ( m w ) + i ) .

In words, the path along which we advanced more at the end of stage 2 is “killed.” We continue advancing along the other path until we reach the final target (which is the target special vertex in Mw+1).

3.3. The cost analysis.

Let us scale uniformly the edge weights in Mw+1, so the diameter of any copy of Mw becomes equal to 1 (this is just for notational simplicity). In particular, the optimal cost is 3mw. Let us assume by induction that we have proved for Mw a lower bound of Cw on the competitive ratio of any deterministic algorithm against the random sequence ρw. We now analyze the cost of any deterministic algorithm in the three stages of the random sequence ρw+1.

Stage 1.

Here, by induction, the expected cost is lower bounded by mwCw.

Stage 2.

Assume that mw≥Cw. (This is a somewhat stricter assumption than seems to be needed here, but we will need this stricter condition later.) Then we claim the expected cost in this stage is lower bounded by mw2Cw. Indeed, in each new “phase” (where the hard sequence ρw is presented either on the left path or on the right path), the algorithm, with probability 1/2, must choose between traversing a copy of Mw against ρw, at expected cost Cw, or alternatively backtracking (i.e., switching) to the other path (either right away, or after a while) which costs at least 2mw≥Cw. This tentatively concludes the proof of the claim, up to the minor issue that a priori we do not control the expected cost of traversal of Mw conditioned on the fact that the algorithm does not switch. To see why this might be a problem, consider the fictitious situation (indeed, our request sequence will not be like this) where with probability 1–ϵ the traversal is easy (say cost 0) and with probability ϵ the traversal is hard (say cost 1/ϵ times the expectation). In that case, switching when the hardness of the traversal is revealed might lower the expected cost by a multiplicative factor ϵ. We explain below in Section 3.5 how to deal with this issue and complete the proof of this paragraph’s claim.

Stage 3.

We have min{left(mw),right(mw)}≤32mw–Ω(mw) with high probability (e.g., on account of the Berry-Esseen Inequality). Therefore, with high probability we face in this stage at least 3mw2+Ω(mw) copies of Mw to traverse. Thus, the expected cost of this stage is (3mw2+Ω(mw))Cw.

3.4. Selecting the parameters and conclusion.

Overall, the algorithm pays (3mw+Ω(mw))Cw in expectation, whereas OPT pays just 3mw. Thus, we get the recurrence relation Cw+1≥(1+Ω(1mw))Cw. Clearly, we want to choose mw to be as small as possible. With the constraint mw≥Cw from the stage 2 analysis we obtain

C w + 1 ≥ C w + Ω ( C w ) .

In particular, we easily get by induction Cw≥Ω(w2). Finally, let us calculate |Mw|. We have |Mw+1|≤6mw|Mw|≤6w∏w‘=1wmw‘. As Cw is of order w2, and mw is of order of Cw, we get that |Mw| is of order exp(Cwlogw) for some constant C>0. In particular, if we denote that number by n, we have logn=Cwlogw, so that w=Θ(lognloglogn). To extend the bound to any number of points n‘, simply choose the largest w for which |Mw|≤n‘, and then extend Mw arbitrarily to contain exactly n‘ points (the extra points will be ignored in the request sequence). This concludes the proof of the lower bound up to the conditioning issue in the stage 2 analysis, which we deal with next.

3.5. Escape price.

Here we resolve the issue of controlling the expected cost obtained by induction for a traversal of Mw, when the algorithm is allowed to abort this traversal and switch to the other branch in Mw+1. Switching to the other branch in stage 2, which is the only stage where it is not obvious that aborting cannot help, costs at least 2mw≥2Cw=2diam(Mw)Cw. (Recall that when considering Mw+1, we scale distances so the diameter of each copy of Mw is 1.)

To control this cost, we actually show inductively a lower bound on the competitive ratio of the escape price relaxation of MSS in Mw, rather than on CrandMSS(Mw,|Mw|). Let pw denote the escape price for the game in Mw. We now show by induction that, for pw=2diam(Mw)Cw, the escape price option does not enable an online algorithm facing the hard random sequence ρw to overcome the stated lower bound. This, in turn, will conclude the proof.

The base case is trivial, so let us assume it is true for some w. In Mw+1, the escape price is 2diam(Mw+1)Cw+1=6mwCw+1. (Recall, again, the uniform scaling of distances when considering Mw+1.) Now, assume the algorithm decides to escape (at the induction level w+1), and that this escape happens in some copy of Mw. Using the induction hypothesis, the cost of instead escaping only at the lower induction level w in the aborted copy, but then proceeding to serve the rest of the hard request sequence by going through all the remaining copies of Mw and paying the expected cost there, is at most the following: 2diam(Mw)Cw=2Cw for the escape price, plus mwCw for stage 1, plus mwCw/2 for stage 2, plus 2mwCw for stage 3. Overall, this cost is at most (2+3.5mw)Cw≤6mwCw+1, as mw≥1. In other words, the escape price option on Mw+1 does not add any benefit to the algorithm compared to the escape price option on Mw, and thus by induction it does not enable the algorithm to overcome the lower bound.

4. An Existential Ω(log2N) Lower Bound for MSS

In this section, we refine the bound from the previous section and show the following theorem.

Theorem 5.

For each n∈N, there exists an n-point metric space M such that CrandMSS(M,n–1)=Ω(log2n).

By Proposition 4, this implies that there is no o(log2n)-competitive algorithm for MTS on general n-point metrics, and no o(log2k)-competitive algorithm for kSRV on general metrics. These lower bounds are tight for MTS, and for kSRV at least in the case of (k+1)-point metrics, on account of the known O(log2n) upper bound for MTS on arbitrary n-point metrics.10

To avoid the log2logn divisor in the bound proved in Section 3, we will use only 6 instead of 6mw copies of Mw when constructing Mw+1, so the metric space is smaller. Note that the reason mw needed to be chosen large in Section 3 is to ensure that the cost of switching between the left and right paths is large. The key idea that will enable us to allow smaller switching cost here is that rather than issuing the inductive request sequence in Mw in its entirety each time, we can break it into smaller subsequences (“chunks”) and only issue a single chunk at a time. Since the cost of a chunk is smaller than the cost of the entire inductive sequence, we do not need as large of a switching cost to discourage the algorithm from switching between the left and right paths. A similar idea of decomposing inductive request sequences into chunks is also the key idea that allows us to tighten the universal lower bounds, as shown in the full version of the paper.

Let 0<α<1 and β∈N be constants we determine later. We will show that for every w∈N there exists a metric space Mw=(Mw,dw) with |Mw|≤β·6w where any randomized algorithm for MSS (with request sets of size at most 2w) has competitive ratio at least αw2. The metric space Mw has two special points sw,tw∈Mw we use as the initial and final location of the lower bound instance (i.e., sw is the initial location of the server, and the request sequence will force the server to terminate at tw). The request sequence will be such that an optimal offline algorithm can serve it for cost dw(sw,tw) by moving along a shortest path from sw to tw.

If αw2≤1, the lower bound is trivial and we choose Mw to be β+1 equally spaced points on a line, with sw and tw being the two outermost points.

For larger w, we proceed by induction. Specifically, for w∈N with α(w+1)2>1, we construct Mw+1 by taking six copies of Mw and gluing them together in a circle as shown in Figure 2. We view Mw+1 as consisting of a left path and right path of 3 copies of Mw each. For j∈{1,2,3}, we denote by Mw,L,j=(Mw,L,j,dw) and Mw,R,j=(Mw,R,j,dw) the jth copy of Mw on the left and right, respectively. If p is a (set of) point(s) in Mw, we denote by pL,j and pR,j the corresponding (sets of) points in the respective copy. Some members of the family of metric spaces constructed in this way are depicted in Figure 3.

To prove the lower bound, we construct by induction on w a random request sequence ρ for Mw on which every deterministic online algorithm has expected cost at least αw2dw(sw,tw). However, to construct these sequences, we will require an induction hypothesis that yields stronger and more delicate properties. Roughly, we will require that the random request sequence ρ can be decomposed into m≥αβw2 (random) subsequences ρ1,…,ρm such that any online algorithm’s expected cost on each ρi is at least some ci≈dw(sw,tw)/β, and the expected sum of these ci is at least αw2dw(sw,tw). This will be captured more precisely by Lemma 6.

Terminology and notation.

A chunk is a sequence of requests. We use this term especially for cases where a sequence is meant to be used as a subsequence of a longer sequence. Sometimes we also use the term subchunk instead of chunk to emphasize that a sequence will be used as a subsequence of a chunk, which in turn will be a subsequence of a longer sequence. Recall that in the context of a sequence of chunks ρ1ρ2…ρm, we denote by ρ≤i=ρ1…ρi the concatenation of the first i chunks, and by ρ≤0 an empty sequence. If the ρi are random, we denote by σ(ρ≤i) the σ-algebra generated by ρ≤i. The property that ci is σ(ρ≤i–1)-measurable in the following lemma simply means ci is a function of ρ≤i–1.

Lemma 6.

For every w∈N, there exists a random sequence of chunks ρ1ρ2…ρm for MSS in Mw, and a choice of random variables c1,…,cm, such that for all i=1,…,m the following conditions hold.

  1. The last request of ρm is {tw}.

  2. copt(ρ≤m)=dw(sw,tw).

  3. ci is σ(ρ≤i–1)-measurable.

  4. For every choice of ρ≤i–1 in the sample space, E[calg(ρi|ρ≤i–1)|ρ≤i–1]≥ci

    for any deterministic online algorithm alg, even if an escape price of 2dw(sw,tw) is available on the suffix ρi.

  5. ci∈[dw(sw,tw)2β,3dw(sw,tw)2β].

We briefly argue that Lemma 6 implies Theorem 5.

Proofof Theorem 5.

In the setting of Lemma 6, we have E[calg(ρ≤m)]=E[∑i=1mE[calg(ρi|ρ≤i–1)|ρ≤i–1]]≥E[∑i=1mci]≥αw2d(sw,tw)=αw2copt(ρ≤m).

Due to the symmetry in the metric space Mw, we can achieve cost ratio αw2 also in the opposite direction from tw to sw, so the instance can be repeated indefinitely. Since a randomized algorithm is a random distribution over deterministic algorithms, we conclude that for each randomized algorithm there exists a request sequence of arbitrarily high cost where the ratio between expected online cost and optimal cost is at least αw2. Since α and β are constants and n=|Mw|≤β·6w, we have αw2∈Ω(w2)⊆Ω(log2n).

The proof of Lemma 6 is rather long, so let us first provide a roadmap to its structure. We prove Lemma 6 by induction on w. The base cases of the induction are all w with αw2≤1: Here, the metric space is Mw={0,1,…,β} with the line metric, and sw=0 and tw=β so that dw(sw,tw)=β. 4.1. Constructing subchunks.

Suppose Lemma 6 holds for some fixed w with α·(w+1)2>1. To deduce the properties in Claim 7 from the induction hypothesis, we first describe in this subsection the construction of the subchunks ρ~1,ρ~2,…,ρ~m~ and sizes c~1,…,c~m~. Recall that distances are scaled such that dw(sw,tw)=β.

The request sequence ρ~≤m~ consists of three stages that are executed one after another. In stage j, requests will only involve points in Mw,L,j∪Mw,R,j.

Stage 1.

Sample a sequence of chunks in Mw by the induction hypothesis, and replace each request set u⊆Mw in it by uL,1∪uR,1⊆Mw,L,1∪Mw,R,1. The sequence obtained this way constitutes the start of our sequence of subchunks ρ~1,ρ~2,…, and we define the size c~i of each subchunk of stage 1 to be equal to the size of the corresponding chunk from which it is created.

Stage 2.

Invoking the induction hypothesis two more times, sample independently two sequences of chunks ρL,1,…,ρL,mL and ρR,1,…,ρR,mR in Mw,L,2 and Mw,R,2, respectively, and let cL,i,cR,i∈[12,32] be the corresponding sizes.

To construct a subchunk in stage 2, we repeatedly do the following: Select a chunk from one of the two inductively constructed sequences of chunks, say ρL,i, and replace in it each request set by the union of itself and the set u of points on the other side (i.e., on the right when the selected chunk is ρL,i) contained in the last request set of the previous subchunk. We then say the construction of this subchunk uses chunk ρL,i. The chunk used to construct a subchunk in this way is always the first unused chunk from either the left or the right (with the side determined randomly in a way described shortly). Thus, each subchunk advances the request sequence on one of the two sides by one chunk, incurring cost for any algorithm that has its server on that side, whereas an algorithm would pay cost 0 for the subchunk if it has its server on the other side (since it would already be at a point of u).

Let left(j) and right(j) be the number of chunks used on the left and right for the construction of the first j chunks of stage 2 (so left(j)+right(j)=j). Let

n L , j : = c L , left ( j – 1 ) + 1 and n R , j : = c R , right ( j – 1 ) + 1

be the sizes of the next unused chunks on the two sides immediately before the construction of subchunk j of stage 2. These are the two candidate chunks for use in the construction of subchunk j. Then the construction of the jth subchunk of stage 2 uses the next unused chunk on the left with probability pL,j, and it uses the next unused chunk on the right otherwise (with probability pR,j=1–pL,j), where

p L , j : = n R , j n L , j + n R , j and p R , j : = n L , j n L , j + n R , j .

These probabilities are chosen so that if Lj:=∑i=1left(j)cL,i and Rj:=∑i=1right(j)cR,i are the total sizes of chunks used on the left and right, respectively, for the first j subchunks of stage 2, then for Sj:=Lj–Rj, the sequence (Sj)j=1,2,… is a martingale. We set the size of the jth subchunk to be nL,jnR,j/(nL,j+nR,j).

These steps continue until the number of subchunks created in stage 2 is

κ = min { k : ∑ j = 1 k + 1 n L , j n R , j ≥ α β w 2 4 } . (1)

Note that it can be checked after the construction of each subchunk whether this stopping condition is satisfied, as it only depends on random choices made beforehand. Since each summand nL,jnR,j≥14 (as the inductive hypothesis assumes Property 5 of Lemma 6), we have κ<αβw2≤min{mL,mR}. Thus, the stopping condition is reached before running out of chunks.

We refer to these first κ subchunks of stage 2 as stage 2a, and the following part as stage 2b: The subchunks of stage 2b are simply the unused chunks on the side whose total size of used chunks in stage 2a was smaller, and the other side gets “killed”. More precisely, if Lκ≤Rκ then the subchunks of stage 2b are ρL,left(κ)+1,ρL,left(κ)+2,…,ρL,mL, and otherwise they are ρR,right(κ)+1,ρR,right(κ)+2,…,ρR,mR. The corresponding sizes are the ones given by the induction hypothesis.

Stage 3.

The last request of stage 2b was either {tw,L,2}={sw,L,3} or {tw,R,2}={sw,R,3}. In the former case, the subchunks and sizes of stage 3 are obtained by invoking the induction hypothesis in Mw,L,3, and otherwise in Mw,R,3.

4.2. Analysis

Let ρ~1,…,ρ~m~ and c~1,…,c~m~ be the entire sequences of subchunks and sizes constructed in stages 1, 2, and 3. The first three properties in Claim 7 follow immediately from the construction and the induction hypothesis of Lemma 6. In particular, an optimal offline algorithm can serve the request sequence for cost 3β by moving through the three copies of Mw on the side (left or right) where stages 2b and 3 are played.

Property 4 follows easily from the induction hypothesis if ρ~i belongs to stage 1, 2b, or 3. If ρ~i belongs to stage 2a, say it is the jth subchunk of stage 2a, then suppose the algorithm is on the left side right before this subchunk is issued. (The case that the algorithm is on the right is symmetric.) With probability pL,j, the subchunk is constructed using the next unused inductive chunk on the left. Conditioned on this being the case, the algorithm pays expected cost at least nL,j for this subchunk by the induction hypothesis. Indeed, even if the algorithm switches to a point in u (the set on the right included in each request) in order to avoid paying more cost for the subchunk, switching to u costs at least 2β, which is the escape price granted by the induction hypothesis. As the event we conditioned on has probability pL,j, the (unconditioned) expected cost of the algorithm for the subchunk is at least pL,jnL,j=nL,jnR,j/(nL,j+nR,j). This is precisely the size of this subchunk by definition, proving property 4.

The property c~i∈[0,32] is immediate from the induction hypothesis for stages 1, 2b, and 3, recalling β=dw(sw,tw). For stage 2a, it also holds because the size of the jth subchunk is nL,jnR,j/(nL,j+nR,j)≤max{nL,j,nR,j}≤32.

Finally, and most crucially, we wish to show that

E [ ∑ i = 1 m ~ c ~ i ] ≥ 3 α β ( w + 1 ) 2 + 3 . (2)

By construction and the induction hypothesis, the expected subchunk sizes sum to at least αβw2 in stage 1, αβw2–E[min{Lκ,Rκ}] in stage 2b, and αβw2 in stage 3. To analyze stage 2a, recall the definitions Lj:=∑i=1left(j)cL,i and Rj:=∑i=1right(j)cR,i and Sj:=Lj–Rj. Notice that the size of the jth subchunk of stage 2a, which is nL,jnR,j/(nL,j+nR,j)=pL,jnL,j, is precisely equal to the expectation of Lj–Lj–1 (conditioned on prior randomness). Thus, the expected sum of chunk sizes in stage 2a is E[Lκ], which by symmetry is equal to E[Rκ] and thus equal to 12E[Lκ+Rκ]. Combining these lower bounds for all stages, we obtain

E [ ∑ i = 1 m ~ c ~ i ] ≥ 3 α β w 2 – E [ min { L κ , R κ } ] + 1 2 E [ L κ + R κ ] = 3 α β w 2 + 1 2 E [ | S κ | ] .

By lower bounding E[|Sκ|] using bounds on the convergence rate in the martingale central limit theorem, we can deduce Inequality 2 and Claim 7, details of which are given in the full version of our paper.

4.3. Combining subchunks.

To complete the proof of the induction step of Lemma 6, the remaining idea is simple: The overall request sequence ρ≤m is identical to the request sequence ρ~≤m~ guaranteed by Claim 7, but we combine some consecutive groups of subchunks into single chunks so their sizes lie in [32,92] instead of [0,32]. Doing so carefully ensures all properties of the induction step of Lemma 6 are satisfied. We omit the details from this extended abstract.
